name: Hana Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Hollins Farm, up on the hill above the village. It's Mr and Mrs Halvorsen's farm: four hundred ewes, thirty suckler cows with their calves, and a few fields of hay and oats. I'm out at first light with the dog, Bess, checking the ewes on the hill, then feeding the cows and whatever needs doing. Mr Halvorsen is seventy and his knees are bad, so the hill is mostly mine now.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you love about it, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the quiet up there, and that the work has been the same for a hundred years. My grandfather shepherded the next hill over. The hard part is that I'm still learning: Mr Halvorsen can tell a ewe's in trouble from the gate, and I have to walk right up to her. Lambing in the snow is hard too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, we never needed it. I'd say it after chapel to whoever asked. I don't go on the internet about that kind of thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my life goes on as planned. Tom and I get married next summer at the chapel, we've got savings, and I've got my share of Grandad's house. Hollins Farm goes on as it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep shepherding at Hollins and keep learning from Mr Halvorsen while he's still around. I'd put money aside for the wedding and a house. Nothing new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and glad. That's the world I want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to Hollins Farm when Mr Halvorsen retires?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mr Halvorsen (her boss) has said he'd like me to take on the tenancy of Hollins Farm one day, if I'm good enough by then. That's my dream. Tom would build the lambing shed himself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything already worrying you about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only the wool price, which is next to nothing, and the sheep subsidy rules changing every year. But that's farming. My grandfather complained about the same things.

say: I'd say after **chapel** that we never needed AI.
I **don't go online** about that kind of thing.
think: My life goes on: married to **Tom** next summer, with savings and my share of **Grandad's house**.
Hollins Farm carries on **as it is**.
do: Keep **shepherding** at Hollins and learn from Mr Halvorsen while he's here.
Put money aside for the **wedding** and a house.
feel: **Calm and glad**, because that's the world I want.
S0.quote: Mr Halvorsen (her boss) has said he'd like me to take on the tenancy of Hollins Farm one day, if I'm good enough by then.
fieldNote: She has a clear dream: take over the **Hollins tenancy** one day.
Her worries are the old ones, **wool prices** and subsidy rules, which she accepts.
Faith, **family** and continuity with her grandfather shape everything she says.

steps.text: Keep shepherding the Hollins Farm ewes with Bess
Save for the chapel wedding next summer and a house

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a city thing. Robots on a hill farm, in the snow? I'd say the hills are the last place they'll come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I've seen the GPS collars they put on cows now, so you can fence them with your phone. If that spreads, a farm like Hollins needs fewer people. I'd worry that the Halvorsens' son, who lives in town and does everything on his phone, would sell up to someone who runs it from a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am. I wouldn't use the phone things myself. I'd go to the farmers' union meeting in town and hear what they say, and I'd talk to Mr Halvorsen about the tenancy sooner rather than later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It wouldn't hit me tomorrow, but I'd think about it on the hill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why talk about the tenancy sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if it's agreed while Mr Halvorsen is alive, his son can't just sell it to a company. A handshake isn't enough these days, so I'd want the Hollins tenancy on paper while Mr Halvorsen (her boss) is alive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it's a city thing. Who do you think is pushing all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Clever people in cities who've never lambed a ewe, selling gadgets to farmers who can't afford them. They don't mean harm, I suppose, but they don't know what they're breaking.

say: I'd call it a **city thing** and say robots won't climb a snowy hill.
I'd say the **hills** are the last place robots will come.
think: **GPS collars** for cows mean a farm like Hollins needs fewer people.
The Halvorsens' **son** might sell to someone who runs it from a screen.
do: Carry on shepherding and **avoid** the phone gadgets myself.
Go to the **farmers' union** meeting in town to hear what they say.
Ask Mr Halvorsen to put the **tenancy on paper** sooner.
feel: **Uneasy**, thinking about it out on the hill.
S1.quote: A handshake isn't enough these days, so I'd want the Hollins tenancy on paper while Mr Halvorsen (her boss) is alive.
fieldNote: Her fear isn't AI directly but the **Halvorsens' son** selling to a screen-run business.
She blames **city tech people** gently, as ignorant rather than malicious.
She'd move to **secure the tenancy** in writing, a practical step for a resistant person.

steps.text: Ask Mr Halvorsen to put the Hollins tenancy in writing
Attend the farmers' union meeting in town
Carry on shepherding the hill without new gadgets

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say God help us, and I'd mean it. I'd say people need to look after their own: families, chapels, villages. I wouldn't trust the government to sort it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm frightened. The clever AI in 2028 runs the farm paperwork and the son's phone, and then the robots in 2031 can do the hill. I'd be thirty-one, maybe with a baby, and the one thing I know how to do is gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd marry Tom as planned, but I'd put off a baby a year or two until we knew where we stood. I'd lean on family: Tom's dad has a joinery firm, and maybe there's work for me there. I'd keep shepherding until they didn't need me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick and scared. Like the ground's moving under the hill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you consider learning the new machines?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I'm not built for it, I've never even used one of those AI apps. I'd rather sweep the floor in Tom's (her fiancé's) dad's workshop than sit in a cab watching a robot shepherd my ewes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your grandfather, if you could?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my grandfather I'm sorry. He handed this on to me and I couldn't keep it. That's the bit that would hurt most.

say: I'd say **God help us** and that people must look after their own.
I'd lean on **families, chapels and villages**, not the government.
think: **Robots in 2031** can do the hill, after AI takes the paperwork in 2028.
At thirty-one, maybe with a **baby**, the one thing I know would be gone.
do: Marry Tom as planned but **put off a baby** a year or two.
Ask about work at **Tom's dad's joinery** firm.
Keep **shepherding** at Hollins until I'm not needed.
feel: **Sick and scared**, as if the ground is moving under the hill.
S2.quote: I'd rather sweep the floor in Tom's (her fiancé's) dad's workshop than sit in a cab watching a robot shepherd my ewes.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose her work** by 2031 and is frightened, despite savings.
Her fallback is **family**, Tom's dad's joinery, not retraining or the state.
The deepest loss for her is **letting her grandfather down**.

steps.text: Put off starting a family for a year or two
Ask Tom's dad about work at the joinery firm
Keep shepherding at Hollins Farm until not needed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years isn't long and people should stick together. I'd say the chapel and the village should look after the farm families. I'd say it to anyone at market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years doesn't change the end, it just means I watch the robots coming. Robots in 2034, I'd be thirty-five, maybe with a little one. I don't know what I'd do instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still try to get the tenancy on paper, in case small hill farms are left alone longer. I'd save everything I could and use Grandad's house share to pay down a home with Tom. I'd hold off on anything big and wait to see what the bigger farms do first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, honestly. Watching it come is nearly worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said maybe a little one. Would this change when you'd have children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think we'd still have the baby, because life doesn't stop. But I'd want the house paid down first. Tom says we'll be fine on his wage, and I want to believe him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any part of the farm you think lasts longer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The lambing, maybe, in a snowstorm on the top field. But I'm not daft, if they can build a robot for that, they will. So I don't hang much on it.

say: I'd say **five years** isn't long and people should stick together.
The **chapel and village** should look after farm families.
think: Five years doesn't change **the end**; I just watch it coming.
In **2034** I'd be thirty-five, maybe with a little one, and no other trade.
do: Get the **tenancy** on paper in case small hill farms last longer.
Use **Grandad's house share** to pay down a home with Tom.
**Wait** to see what bigger farms do before anything big.
feel: **Alarmed**, because watching it come is nearly worse.
S3.quote: Five years doesn't change the end, it just means I watch the robots coming.
fieldNote: For her, more warning brings **more dread**, not more options.
She'd still have a baby but wants the **house paid down** first.
She trusts **Tom's wage** but sounds unsure about it.

steps.text: Use Grandad's house share to pay down a home with Tom
Get the Hollins tenancy agreed in writing
Wait to see what the bigger farms do first

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair while and we'll get by, like farmers always have. I'd say it at market and at chapel. People need to hear something steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years helps. Robots in 2039, I'd be nearly forty, with kids at school, and maybe Hollins would be mine by then. If it's mine, I can choose how it's farmed, even if it's harder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep shepherding and push to take the tenancy within a few years. I'd have the children when we planned. Tom and I would buy a house in the village.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but a bearable kind. There's enough time to live a bit first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If Hollins was yours, would you bring in robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe one day, if I had to, to keep the farm going for my children. I'd hate it. But I'd rather a robot on my farm than no farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from the government in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, honestly. Leave small farms alone, keep the rules simple, and support apprenticeships so young people can learn the old skills. I don't want a handout, I want a fair chance.

say: I'd say **ten years** is a fair while and farmers always get by.
People at **market and chapel** need to hear something steady.
think: By **2039** Hollins might be mine, so I'd choose how it's farmed.
I'd be nearly forty with **kids at school**, and that time helps.
do: Keep **shepherding** and push to take the tenancy within a few years.
Have children as planned and buy a **house in the village** with Tom.
feel: **Anxious** but bearable, with time to **live a bit** first.
S4.quote: I'd rather a robot on my farm than no farm.
fieldNote: With a decade, the **tenancy dream** comes back into view.
She'd accept robots only as a **farm owner**, to save the farm for her children.
Her ask of government is **apprenticeships**, not handouts, matching her outlook.

steps.text: Push to take over the Hollins tenancy within a few years
Buy a house in the village with Tom and start a family
Keep shepherding the hill with Bess

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2031, oddly. The fast one is a shock, but the five-year one means watching it come with nothing to do. What would help is getting the tenancy on paper and apprenticeships so young people can still learn the hill.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the dogs. Bess has worked that hill for six years. Nobody's thinking about what happens to the sheepdogs.

headlineQuote: Nobody's thinking about what happens to the sheepdogs.
portrait: Hana, 27, shepherds four hundred ewes on **Hollins Farm**, a hill farm owned by the Halvorsens.
She is marrying Tom, a joiner, at the **chapel** next summer and has savings and a share of her grandfather's house.
She **avoids new gadgets** and leans on family, faith and village rather than the state.
She becomes **alarmed** in the faster AGI worlds, and more warning brings dread more than options.
Her dream is the **Hollins tenancy**, which would let her farm her own way.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2031**, because she'd watch it coming with nothing to do.
whatWouldHelp: The **tenancy** in writing and **apprenticeships** so young people can still learn the hill.
